Albanese's end of year message
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has capped off the morning with a traditional valedictory address.
He reflected on the past year and impact on the Bondi attack and the rise in violent rhetoric towards politicians.
"I do hope everyone has a very safe festival season and a beautiful summer. I certainly hope it's a more restful summer than the last one was for Australia, which was a devastating period," he says.
"For the Jewish community, this will be a difficult time coming up. I will be attending commemorations on December 4 and December 6.
"(Our) thoughts are with the people who've been lost to us — but for the families, friends, and community who lost 16 Australians at that time, our thoughts will be very much with you."
Albanese says the alleged attack on Indi MP Helen Haines shows we are now living in "insecure times".
The parliament is now adjourned and will return at midday on February 2, 2027.

Coalition tries to make last minute tweaks to gas reservation scheme
Let's check in on the progress of the gas reservation scheme voting.
Manager of Opposition Business Dan Tehan has put up a number of fresh amendments from the Coalition.
He argues since it's so bright and early and every one in the chamber is "alert and listening" it's the right time to debate it.
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese thinks otherwise. He confirms the government won't be supporting the amendments (meaning they won't pass).
The bells ring and the votes continue to roll on.
'We'd have the Nationals Party tattooed on our arms': McKenzie
Nationals frontbencher Bridget McKenzie is clearly not impressed by Leah Blyth's defection to One Nation.
Blyth revealed on the final sitting day of the year she would be making the switch from the Liberals to Pauline Hanson's party. McKenzie says people are "sick of" elected MPs and senators defecting.

"I think when you look at all of these scenarios and you think about why an MP has defected to a different party, some of those are significant, unresolvable personality clashes, but most of them ... actually think they've got better electoral prospects with their new home," she tells ABC's Radio National Breakfast.
"I think may mail is Australians are feeling pretty ripped off when people do that."
Yesterday, Nationals leader Matt Canavan confessed some within the party had the wobbles. McKenzie says she hasn't had to talk anyone out of leaving.

"We're all sort of, if we're into tattoos, we'd have the National Party tattooed on our arms because we are born and bred and we believe our political movement has a significant role to play in the modern Australian democracy," she says.
Get out the tattoo gun!
Aged care changes will undergo further review: Butler
Health Minister Mark Butler has acknowledged the government's aged care overhaul will require further review.

A year after Labor's sweeping aged care changes took effect, a Senate committee has recommended the health department review the amount elderly Australians pay towards their Support at Home services, such as cleaning.

Senators from across the parliament also called on the government to "immediately" change the law to allow for humans to override "at the point of assessment" the algorithms used in the assessment process.
Butler says he's committed to ensuring older Australians get all the care and support they need.
"We're reviewing the tool, the priority mechanism we passed only in the last several weeks to provide a new review mechanism for people with complex needs."
The bells are ringing on the gas reservation scheme
Action is about to kick off in the lower house. MPs are slowly making their way to the chamber to work through the final votes on the gas reservation scheme.
I'll keep my eyes on the chamber and let you know if anything exciting happens.
King won't set target price under gas reservation scheme
Resources Minister Madeleine King won't put a price tag on how much the gas reservation scheme would reduce energy bills by.

The gas reservation, which would require gas exporters to reserve up to 20 per cent of its supply for domestic use, is set to pass the parliament this morning after the Coalition agreed to wave it through.
King tells ABC Radio National Breakfast doing so will put downward pressure on prices for individuals and industry. But she's reluctant to put a figure on it.
Rather, she's happy to use the $12 cap set under the gas market code of conduct as a benchmark.
"We want to drive prices down to at least that," she says."We aren't setting a figure because we don't want that figure to then become the floor, which is what happens with a cap."
"We want to drive prices down to at least that," she says.
"We aren't setting a figure because we don't want that figure to then become the floor, which is what happens with a cap."
Fellow SA Lib brands Blyth defection 'an absolute betrayal'

The senator sensationally quit the party to join One Nation in the final sitting week of the year. Blyth, a former state Liberal president, was appointed to the Senate last year to fill the vacancy left by Simon Birmingham.
On his way into parliament this morning, Venning told reporters he didn't see her defection coming.
"She wasn't elected. She came in on a vacancy from Simon Birmingham. People voted for the Liberal Party. She's jumped ship to One Nation. It's an absolute betrayal," he said.
Shoebridge says gas reservation scheme a 'distraction' from need for gas export tax
Greens Leader David Shoebridge says Labor's gas reservation scheme is designed to push back against a campaign for a tax on gas exports.
Shoebridge says 70 per cent of Australians support the idea of a 20 per cent tax on gas exports, to get a "fair share" for of the country's resources.
"It's no coincidence that the Labor government announced this gas reservation scheme off the back of a really powerful campaign to get that gas tax," he said.
He says there are figures within the gas industry who are not entirely pleased with the gas reservation scheme, but certainly prefer it to the alternative.
"I can tell you this, they bloody well prefer it to the actual reform that's needed, which is a gas export tax," he says.
"We see this as a distraction, a very clear distraction".
Wait, Harry who?
It's the big day! No, I'm not talking about the gas reservation scheme passing parliament this morning. It's Harry Styles concert day.
While this is big news to people like me (millennials who a decade on still have One Direction in their Spotify Wrapped) … it's not so much to others like Liberal senator Dave Sharma.
"I have to say ... I think I had to look him up when you told me you wanted to ask about this ... to make sure I knew what he looked like in case you showed photos," Sharma confessed to Nine.
Yeah, that's why I'm Googling him too, ABC bosses, if you ask.
Greens deputy Steph Hodgins-May doesn't have tickets to his show but is enjoying seeing all the pics of him popping up in Melbourne's south side.
What would she ask him if she ran into him? Whether he agreed with Elton John's call to restrict AI access to intellectual property of Australian artists without full permission.
"I'll be keeping an eye out for him and his little red hot shorts."
House of Reps to return at 8am!
It was a late night in the Senate as it worked its way through amendments to the gas reservation scheme.
That means the lower house MPs had to spend another night in Canberra in order the to cast the final vote before it becomes law.
How fun!
Key Event
'Self-serving': Sharma joins Libs ripping into One Nation defector
Liberal MPs certainly aren't holding back on what they think about SA senator Leah Blyth's defection to One Nation.

The former Liberal sensationally revealed the news yesterday, on the final sitting day of the year. Two of her colleagues, Ben Small and Garth Hamilton, told The Australian newspaper that Blyth had "openly mocked" Pauline Hanson and the party as recently as this week.
Asked by Nine if Blyth had made any comments to him, Liberal senator Dave Sharma says she never said anything positive.
"I certainly never saw any evidence of her having any attraction to One Nation or say anything positive about them," he says.
"I think it's pretty transparent if you saw her press conference yesterday that this was an action that was self-serving, self-interested, and frankly pretty dishonourable."
Ouch.
Report recommends human oversight for controversial aged care funding algorithm

Co-payments elderly Australians make towards the subsidised care they receive at home should be reviewed and clinicians should be able to override controversial assessment algorithms, a parliamentary committee has found.

A year on from the federal government's aged care overhaul, a Senate committee has recommended the Health Department review the amount elderly Australians pay towards their Support at Home services, such as cleaning, food preparation or gardening.
Key Event
Former premier says gas reservation policy one of best things economically for WA
Former Western Australian premier Alan Carpenter says a national gas reservation scheme is long overdue.
Parliament has been extended this morning to allow the national scheme's legislation to pass, after it was rubber stamped in the Senate last night.
The reforms include a carve-out for Western Australia, which has had its own gas reservation scheme since 2006.
Carpenter says the national version is "20 years too late".

"The decision to impose a 15 per cent domestic gas reservation policy on the oil and gas industry off the west coast of Australia is one of the best things, as it's turned out, that has ever happened economically to WA," he said.
"Since we imposed that requirement, there's been, I don't know, 100 billion dollars of foreign investment into oil and gas industry off the coast of WA".
Good morning 👋
Hello friends. Welcome to our politics live blog. I'm Courtney Gould from the ABC's Parliament House team, here to guide you through the day.

After a long week, and a late night in the Senate, the final sitting of the year is almost over. Lower house MPs will return to the chamber this morning to rubber stamp amendments to the gas reservation scheme (more on that shortly).
Focus will now turn to Victorian election tomorrow and the towards the Mid-Year Economic and Fiscal Outlook.
Let's not beat around the bush and let's get blogging.
